title: What environmental soil boring data needs to survive an audit
summary: A soil boring log holds up in an audit when every entry shows who recorded it, where, when, and with what. Here’s what every log needs.
body_markdown:
A soil boring log can get the geology right and still fall apart in an environmental audit. If a reviewer can’t tell who recorded a value, when, or with which meter, the log starts to wobble. Many of those answers exist only at the boring and vanish once the rig pulls out. See what a defensible log needs, and how Fulcrum captures every entry at the rig with its trail intact.


**Key insights**


- Regulatory audits of Phase II environmental soil boring logs collapse over missing timestamps and mismatched chain-of-custody sample IDs rather than flawed geologic descriptions.
- Retyping paper field logs into office software or writing down drilling depths from memory turns valid boring data into unverifiable reconstructions.
- Environmental screening measurements like PID vapor readings are legally defenseless without recording the specific meter ID and pre- and post-use calibration checks.
- Regulatory compliance requires every soil log correction to preserve a visible, dated audit trail instead of overwriting original values in spreadsheets.
- Borehole data such as drill method switches, sample recovery rates, and water levels must be documented at the rig in real time before the driller departs.


A soil boring log can describe the geology perfectly and still fall apart in an audit. Trouble can start in the entries around the description: a missing timestamp, an unrecorded meter, a mismatched sample ID. In a Phase II environmental site assessment or other subsurface investigation, each entry needs a person, place, time, and instrument behind it.


Many of those answers exist only at the boring, while the rig is still turning. An environmental audit or agency review can show up months later, long after anyone could go back and check. The logs that hold up carry their provenance from the first push to the last sample.


## Where boring logs break down under review


Provenance slips away one entry at a time, somewhere between the rig and the report. Each slip looks minor on the day and turns into a question once a reviewer starts tracing values. The five below show how quickly a solid log can lose its footing under review.


- **Depths entered from memory.** A number scribbled down in the truck after the rig pulls out carries no timestamp at all. A reviewer can’t tell that observation from a reconstruction, and neither can the geologist six months later.
- **Field screening readings with no instrument record.** A photoionization detector (PID) reading means little until anyone checking it knows which meter took it. The instrument ID and calibration record show whether that meter read accurately on the day.


- **Method changes that never reach the log.** Switching from direct push drilling to hollow stem auger at 12 feet changes how every deeper sample comes up. A log that skips the switch tells the wrong story about every sample below it.
- **Sample IDs that drift from the chain-of-custody form.** One transposed digit between the log and the chain of custody form can orphan a lab result. The value then floats free of the interval it came from, along with everything it was meant to prove.
- **Corrections typed over the original.** An overwritten spreadsheet cell shows only the latest value, with no trace of the first one. Anyone opening the final file can’t see what changed, when, or who changed it.


All five failures thrive in a process built on paper sheets and retyping. When a geologist completes a paper sheet from notes that evening, the timing of every entry disappears. Retyping that sheet into boring log software then adds a second author to every line. The finished file looks clean, but it keeps no record of the handoff that produced it.


## What a defensible soil boring log usually includes


Requirements for boring logs vary by agency, state, and project, so no one list covers them all. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers offers a solid example in its[manual for boring and monitoring wells at hazardous waste sites](https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/tr/pdf/ADA402103.pdf) . The manual applies to Corps teams and their contractors, including those on Corps-managed Superfund cleanups. Most of the entries below follow its lead, and each one answers a question a reviewer is likely to ask.


- **Boring identity.** Each boring gets its own number and a spot on a site sketch inside the log. Keeping that number fixed means every sample and reading stays tied to the right hole.
- **Location and reference datum.** Coordinates and ground surface elevation mean little unless the log names the map system they’re measured against. Mixing up an old system with the current one can[put a boring 10 to 100 meters off](https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/how-large-north-american-datum-1927-nad-27-nad-83-shift) . At that distance, a soil boring can land on the wrong side of a property line.
- **Start and end times.** The log records when drilling started and finished, plus which crew was working when. A reviewer can then match each sample to the shift that collected it.
- **Drill rig and method.** The log names the drilling rig, the drilling contractor, the drilling method, and the depth of any change in method. A switch partway down changes how deeper samples come up, so the record has to show it.
- **Sample recovery.** For each sample, the log notes the sample number and interval, how far the sampler (such as a split spoon or direct push liner) went and how much soil came back, plus blow counts for driven samplers. A short return means the sample only represents part of the interval it came from.
- **Soil descriptions.** The geologist describes each sample in the field, using a standard classification system such as the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS), while it’s still in hand. A description written later from memory or photos carries far less weight with a reviewer.
- **Groundwater.** The log records the depth where water first showed up and how the geologist measured it, along with later water levels. A reading right after drilling can look very different from a reading the next morning.
- **Field screening readings.** Vapor meter readings go on the log at each sample interval with the meter’s make, model, and serial number. A reviewer can then tell exactly which instrument produced each number on the page.


A project’s quality assurance project plan (QAPP) or state program may add more entries to that list. Whatever the rulebook, each entry does one job: tracing a value back to the moment someone recorded it. A log that does that line by line can stand up to whichever reviewer comes next.


## The entries only the field can supply


Project teams can rebuild some entries on soil boring logs later from invoices, survey files, or lab reports. But others exist only at the boring, in the minutes between one core coming out and the next push. Once the rig pulls out, those entries turn into whatever somebody remembers about the day.


EPA Region 4’s Laboratory Services and Applied Science Division tackles that problem head-on in a[logbooks procedure](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-06/documents/Logbooks.pdf) for its own staff. Its rules call for recording observations as they happen, with every entry dated and signed or initialed. By that standard, a value written up over dinner is a reconstruction, however careful the person writing it. Field staff also note any QAPP deviation in the logbook while still in the field, before anyone writes the report. The procedure even accepts electronic records as originals, provided nobody jotted them on paper first.


Even a reading logged the moment it happens can be wrong if the meter behind it is off. Meters lose accuracy gradually, and a bad reading looks just as solid on the log as a good one.


Checking the meter before and after use exposes any slippage, and EPA’s procedure requires both checks and the meter ID. For consultants on state-led projects, the state sets those rules, and some states go further. For example, Florida requires every field reading to sit between a passing check before sampling and a passing check after it. When a vapor meter fails its closing check, every reading since the last passing check gets[flagged as qualified data](https://floridadep.gov/sites/default/files/Equip_Calibration_Guidance.pdf) . Florida’s rules then attach a qualifier code to each of those values in the report.


Under EPA procedure, corrections leave a trail too, so a fixed value never erases the original. On paper, a mistake gets one line through it, plus a date and initials, so the original stays readable. In electronic files, each edit needs a note explaining it, with the date and the initials of whoever made it. Anyone reviewing the record can see the old value, the new one, and who made the call.


Put together, those rules describe a solid record: written on the spot, by a named person, with changes visible. A depth written down from memory fails that test, even if the number turns out to be right.


## Following one boring from rig setup to report table


A paper or spreadsheet boring log passes through several hands on its way from the rig to the report. Each handoff is a chance to lose a timestamp, garble a sample ID, or overwrite a correction. Fulcrum cuts out those handoffs by capturing each entry at the boring, upstream of logging software and lab systems.


[Environmental teams](https://www.fulcrumapp.com/industries/environmental/) build their own boring logs in Fulcrum, with required fields for soil descriptions and classifications, sampling intervals, blow counts, and borehole records. A missing value shows up at the boring, while the geologist can still fill it in.


At rig setup, the geologist opens a record that captures the boring’s location and a timestamp. From there, Fulcrum’s[ArcGIS integration](https://www.fulcrumapp.com/geospatial-capabilities/) carries that point straight into the project’s GIS layers. Capture works offline on sites with no signal, and the record syncs once the device reconnects.


As drilling proceeds, the geologist logs each interval and soil layer with its soil description and recovery. Each interval also carries a timestamped photo of the core that came out of it. When the driller switches methods at 12 feet, for example, the change goes in as its own entry.


PID readings sit right beside the instrument ID and calibration record for the meter that took them. Sample IDs go in at the interval where each sample came out of the ground, ready to match the laboratory analysis that comes back later. Record-level history shows what changed and who changed it, so corrections someone makes when off site stay visible.


In the office, borehole summaries, site maps, and tables of subsurface conditions come straight from the structured data. Report values link back to the original soil sample, so any number traces to its interval.

There was a lot of room for error, and many layers of redundant communications,” said Colin Diehl, the firm’s CEO and co-founder. Moving those records into Fulcrum changed what stays behind when experienced staff move on. “Even with senior folks retiring, we still have this layer of documentation that remains,” he said. “We can always start where we left off, and know the data is available.”


Across projects,[Fulcrum Insights](https://www.fulcrumapp.com/blog/fulcrum-insights-turning-field-data-into-answers/) can answer plain-language questions about those records, like which sites logged stained soil. The same structured capture extends to other[environmental remediation workflows](https://www.fulcrumapp.com/resources/webinar/streamlining-swppp-esa-and-remediation-workflows/) , from site assessments to groundwater sampling.


By the time a boring entry reaches the report table, every value from it carries its own history. Depth, meter, sample ID, and the person behind each entry all sit in one record. Nobody has to rebuild anything from memory, because the geologist logged every entry on the spot.


## A boring log that holds up months later


An audit goes through a boring log entry by entry, long after the drilling ends. The rules differ from agency to agency, and the standard behind each entry barely changes. It comes down to three things: logged in the moment, by a named person, with every change visible. No amount of argument after the fact will conjure a calibration record nobody wrote down.


Much of that record exists only at the boring, and it disappears once the rig pulls out. Firms that capture those entries in the moment hand reviewers soil boring data that answers its own questions. Environmental data validation gets easier too, because every entry already shows where it came from. The project manager who signs the report can answer a reviewer’s question by pointing to the entry behind it.


Geology will always leave room for interpretation, and a well-kept log keeps everything else out of the argument. When the questions finally come, the answers are already sitting in the log, right where the geologist left them.
